LINQ is a set of tools for asking questions about data. Imagine a tray of student cards: keep the passing cards, sort them, then copy only the information you need.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Filter, sort, project and group

var passes = students.Where(s => s.Mark >= 50)
    .OrderBy(s => s.Name)
    .Select(s => new { s.Name, s.Mark });
foreach (var student in passes)
    Console.WriteLine($"Pass: {student.Name} {student.Mark}");
var average = students.Average(s => s.Mark);
var groups = students.GroupBy(s => s.Mark >= 50);

Where filters; OrderBy sorts; Select projects into a small anonymous object. Anonymous types have compiler-generated read-only properties and are useful inside a method. Use named DTOs for API contracts. Expected passing rows: Lefa 80 and Mpho 90.

Deferred execution and database queries

Many LINQ operators describe a query without immediately running it. foreach, ToList, Count and similar terminal operations execute it. A List uses LINQ-to-Objects. An EF IQueryable can translate supported operations into SQL. Do filtering and paging before ToListAsync to avoid loading the whole table. First throws when no match exists; FirstOrDefault can return null. Check for null.

Try it yourself

Return only names for marks 80 and above.

Worked answer

students.Where(s => s.Mark >= 80).Select(s => s.Name). Expected: Lefa, Mpho.

Explain why ToList before Where can waste memory.

Worked answer

It loads every row before filtering. On a database query, filter first and materialize the smaller result.
